items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Put an ice cube in a cup, leave it on the table and observe. Question : (i) What can you conclude from the observations? (ii) Does this mean that ice and water are the same substance?
items.answer: Observation: When you leave an ice cube in a cup on the table, it slowly changes into water. Conclusion: From this observation, we can conclude that ice and water are indeed the same substance. They are just two different forms, or “states,” of the same water. Ice is the solid state of water, and liquid water is the liquid state of water. Activity 8.2 : Let us investigate

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Keep observing this at regular intervals until the water completely disappears. Question : (i) What do you infer? (ii) Is this activity enough to come to the conclusion that water does not seep through a steel plate?
items.answer: Observation: When you put water on a steel plate, you will observe that the water does not go through the plate to the other side. If you leave it for some time, the water will slowly disappear completely. Inference: From this, we can infer that the water did not seep through the steel plate because steel is a solid material and water cannot pass through it. The water disappears because it changes into water vapour (a gas) and mixes with the air. This process is called evaporation. Sufficiency of activity: Yes, this activity is enough to conclude that water does not seep through a solid steel plate. If it had seeped through, the other side of the plate would have become wet, or the water level in the puddle would decrease due to absorption, which doesn’t happen with a steel plate. The disappearance is due to evaporation. Activity 8.3 : Let us experiment

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Record your observations and the questions that arise in your mind. You can also touch the outer surface of the glass tumbler to feel if there is any change.
items.answer: Observation: After a few minutes, you will observe tiny water droplets (like small drops of water) forming on the outer surface of the glass tumbler. When you touch the glass, it will feel wet and cold. Activity 8.4 : Let us measure Aavi and Thirav conduct an activity to find evidence for their reasons. You can also conduct the activity by following the steps given below. Record your data in Table.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Record the time taken for the water to completely evaporate in each case in Table. Table : Findings of the investigation Exposed area of water Time taken for complete evaporation Less (bottle cap) More (plate) (i) What conditions did we keep the same? (ii) What did we change in this investigation? (iii) What did we measure?
items.answer: Observations and Analysis: Time taken for complete evaporation: The water in the plate will evaporate much faster than the water in the bottle cap. Conditions kept the same: (i) The amount of water. (ii) The type of liquid (water). (iii) The surrounding temperature (since they are kept near each other). (iv) The air movement (assuming no fan is used near them). Conditions changed in this investigation: The exposed surface area of the water. The water in the plate has a larger surface area exposed to the air compared to the water in the bottle cap. What we measured: The time taken for the water to completely evaporate in each case. Conclusion: Water evaporates faster when it has a larger surface area exposed to the air. Activity 8.8: Let us explore

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: You can also repeat this activity on a windy or a rainy day, and record your observations.
items.answer: Observations and Conclusions: Sunlight vs. Shade: The water in the cap kept in direct sunlight will evaporate much faster than the water in the cap kept in the shade. This shows that temperature (heat from sunlight) affects the rate of evaporation. Higher temperature leads to faster evaporation. Windy Day: If you repeat this on a windy day, the water will evaporate even faster. This shows that air movement (wind) also speeds up evaporation. Rainy Day: If you repeat this on a rainy day (which usually means more humidity in the air), the water will evaporate slower. This indicates that humidity (amount of water vapour already in the air) affects evaporation. Higher humidity leads to slower evaporation. Overall Conclusion: Evaporation is faster when there is more heat, more air movement (wind), and less humidity in the air. Activity 8.9 : Let us make a model

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: You can also make a drawing of the pot-in- pot cooler once it is ready Allow 4-5 hours for the mini pot-in-pot cooler to cool down. Observe and discuss how it creates a cooling effect inside the pots. Keep some vegetables and fruits in it and observe for a week on a daily basis to check for the freshness of the vegetables and fruits kept inside the cooler. You will have to add water regularly to keep the sand moist. For how many days can the vegetables and fruits be kept fresh in it? What are the conditions which can affect the number of these days? What else can be used in place of sand for better cooling?
items.answer: How it creates a cooling effect: The water you pour in the sand between the two pots seeps through the tiny pores of the earthen pots and the sand. This water then slowly evaporates from the surface of the pots and the wet sand. When water evaporates, it takes heat from its surroundings, which includes the pots and the air inside the inner pot. This removal of heat makes the inside of the cooler (and anything stored in it) feel cold. This is known as the cooling effect of evaporation. Freshness of vegetables and fruits: The vegetables and fruits kept inside the pot- in-pot cooler will stay fresh for a longer time compared to keeping them outside at room temperature. The exact number of days will depend on factors like the type of vegetable/fruit, the outside temperature, and how often you add water. Conditions affecting freshness: Zutside temperature: On hotter days, more evaporation happens, so it might stay cooler but also need more frequent watering. Humidity: In dry weather, evaporation is faster, leading to more cooling. In humid weather, evaporation is slower, so the cooling effect might be less. Regular watering: Keeping the sand moist is crucial for continuous evaporation and cooling. Ventilation: Good airflow around the cooler helps evaporation. What else can be used in place of sand for better cooling: Materials that can hold water and allow it to evaporate slowly would work. Spongy materials or even porous soil could be considered, but sand is commonly used because it holds water well and allows for effective evaporation. Activity 8.10 : Let us engage in a group activity

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What will you observe? Ans : Observation (First part - only water): When you squeeze and release the bottle with just water, you might not see much, or maybe a very faint mist, depending on the air’s humidity. Observation (Second part - with burnt newspaper): When you add a small burnt piece of newspaper and repeat squeezing and releasing, you will observe a noticeable haziness or a cloud- like formation above the water in the bottle. Explanation: The burnt newspaper provides very tiny, invisible dust particles in the bottle. When you squeeze the bottle, the air inside gets compressed and heated slightly. When you release it quickly, the air expands and cools down rapidly. This rapid cooling makes the water vapour (gas) in the air inside the bottle condense (change back to liquid water) around these tiny dust particles, forming many tiny water droplets that appear as a cloud. This activity shows that dust particles act as tiny surfaces for water vapour to condense on, which is important for cloud formation in nature. Activity 8.11 : Let us understand the process Label figure using arrows shown and the words given in the box to show where water is stored, how water changes its state and where it moves. Words to use: Cloud, Lake, Ocean, River, Groundwater, Evaporation, Condensation, Rain, Snow Figure : Change of states and movement of water
items.answer: 1. Ocean / Lake / River : These are places where water is stored on the Earth’s surface. Arrows pointing upwards from these bodies indicate evaporation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Which of the following best describes condensation? (i) The conversion of water into its vapour state. (ii) The process of water changing from a liquid into gaseous state. (iii) The formation of clouds from tiny water droplets. (iv) The conversion of water vapour into its liquid state.
items.answer: (iv) The conversion of water vapour into its liquid state. Condensation always means water vapour cooling and turning back into tiny liquid droplets (e.g., dew on a cold bottle or cloud droplets).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Identify in which of the given processes, evaporation is very important— (i) Colouring with

options.label: A
options.text: crayons

options.label: B
options.text: water colours

options.label: C
options.text: acrylic colours

options.label: D
options.text: pencil colours (ii) Writing on paper with

items.answer: (i) (b) water colours (ii) (b) ink pen Water-colour paint and ink-pen ink dry only when their liquid solvent (mostly water) evaporates; crayons, pencils or ball-pens rely mainly on wax or quick-dry gels, so evaporation is less critical.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: We see green coloured plastic grass at many places these days. Space around natural grass feels cooler than space around the plastic grass. Can you find out why?
items.answer: Natural grass contains water that keeps escaping as vapour (transpiration). Evaporation absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the air above real grass feels cooler. Plastic grass has no water to evaporate, so no cooling occurs.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Give examples of liquids other than water that evaporate.
items.answer: Alcohol (spirit), petrol, perfume, acetone (nail- polish remover).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Fans move air around, creating a cooling sensation. It might seem strange to use a fan to dry wet clothes since fans usually make things cooler, not warmer. Normally, when water evaporates, it requires heat, not cold air. What do you think about this?
items.answer: A fan replaces the moist air next to wet cloth with drier air, so water keeps evaporating. Evaporation needs heat, which it takes from the cloth and room; the clothes dry faster even without warm air.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Usually, when sludge is removed from drains, it is left in heaps next to the drain for 3–4 days. Afterward, it is transported to a garden or a field where it can be used as manure. This approach reduces transportation cost of the sludge and enhances the safety of individuals handling it. Reflect upon it and explain how.
items.answer: When sludge is left near the drain for 3–4 days, it loses water and becomes lighter, so it’s cheaper to transport. In this time, harmful germs reduce, and the bad smell becomes less. This makes it safer and easier for people to handle and better to use as manure in fields or gardens.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Observe the activities in your house for a day. Identify the activities that involve evaporation. How does understanding the process of evaporation help us in our daily activities?
items.answer: At home, I saw evaporation in activities like drying clothes, water drying after mopping, and sweat drying from our skin. Knowing about evaporation helps us dry things faster using heat and air and understand how sweating cools our body.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How is water present in the solid state in nature?
items.answer: Water is present in the solid state in nature as ice. We can see it as snow on mountains, glaciers in polar regions, icebergs floating in the sea and hail during storms. These are all natural forms of solid water.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Reflect on the statement Water is our responsibility before it is our right. Share your thoughts.
items.answer: The statement means we must take care of water before using it freely. Water is precious, and wasting or polluting it can harm everyone. By using it wisely and keeping it clean, we protect it for ourselves and future generations..

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: The seat of a two-wheeler parked on a sunny day has become very hot. How can you cool it down?
items.answer: . To cool down the hot seat of a two-wheeler parked in the sun, you can:

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What are the two forms of the same substance, like ice and water, also called?

options.label: A
options.text: Mixtures

options.label: B
options.text: Solutions

options.label: C
options.text: States

options.label: D
options.text: Compounds

items.answer: (C) States Ice and water are different forms or states of the same substance. These states (solid and liquid in this case) exhibit different physical properties and behaviors.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What happens to an ice cube when it is left on a table at room temperature, as observed in Activity 8.1?

options.label: A
options.text: It evaporates directly into gas

options.label: B
options.text: It gets converted into water

options.label: C
options.text: It remains unchanged indefinitely

options.label: D
options.text: It becomes smaller but stays solid

items.answer: (B) It gets converted into water. Activity 8.1 demonstrates that when an ice cube (solid state of water) is left at room temperature, it absorbs heat from the surroundings and melts, changing into liquid water.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: When water in puddles disappears after some time, where does the water primarily go?

options.label: A
options.text: It seeps entirely into the ground

options.label: B
options.text: It gets converted into water vapour and goes into the air

options.label: C
options.text: It freezes and becomes invisible ice

options.label: D
options.text: It is absorbed by nearby plants completely

items.answer: (B) It gets converted into water vapour and goes into the air. The disappearance of water from puddles or wet surfaces is primarily due to evaporation, where liquid water changes into its gaseous state (water vapour) and mixes with the air.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is evaporation?

options.label: A
options.text: The process of conversion of water vapour into its liquid state

options.label: B
options.text: The process of conversion of water into its solid state (ice)

options.label: C
options.text: The process of conversion of water into its vapour state

options.label: D
options.text: The process of water seeping into the ground

items.answer: (C) The process of conversion of water into its vapour state. Evaporation is defined as the process where a liquid, such as water, changes into its gaseous state, which is called vapour (e.g., water vapour or steam).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is steam actually composed of ?

options.label: A
options.text: Purely invisible water vapour

options.label: B
options.text: Water vapour, with some part converting into tiny visible water droplets

options.label: C
options.text: A different chemical substance than water

options.label: D
options.text: Only hot air mixed with smoke

items.answer: (B) Water vapour, with some part converting into tiny visible water droplets. Steam is essentially water vapour and its visibility is usually the result of some of that vapour condensing into tiny liquid water droplets suspended in the air.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Why do water droplets appear on the outer surface of a glass tumbler containing cold water and ice cubes (Activity 8.3)?

options.label: A
options.text: Water from inside the tumbler seeps through the glass

options.label: B
options.text: Ice from inside melts and leaks out of the glass

options.label: C
options.text: Water vapour from the surrounding air condenses on the cold outer surface

options.label: D
options.text: The glass itself produces water when it becomes cold

items.answer: (C) Water vapour from the surrounding air condenses on the cold outer surface. The cold outer surface of the glass tumbler cools the surrounding air. Water vapour present in this air, upon contacting the cold surface, loses heat and changes from a gas to liquid water droplets.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is condensation?

options.label: A
options.text: The process of conversion of water into its vapour state

options.label: B
options.text: The process of conversion of water vapour into its liquid state

options.label: C
options.text: The process of ice melting into liquid water

options.label: D
options.text: The process of water freezing into ice

items.answer: (B) The process of conversion of water vapour into its liquid state. Condensation is the physical process where a substance in its gaseous state, like water vapour, transforms into its liquid state, such as water droplets, typically due to cooling.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: When a covered glass tumbler with ice water is weighed over time, what happens to its mass, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Mass decreases due to evaporation from inside

options.label: B
options.text: Mass remains exactly the same

options.label: C
options.text: Mass increases due to condensation of water vapour from the air onto the outer surface

options.label: D
options.text: Mass fluctuates randomly due to temperature changes

items.answer: (C) Mass increases due to condensation of water vapour from the air onto the outer surface. As water vapour from the surrounding air condenses into liquid water droplets on the cold outer surface of the tumbler, this added water contributes to an increase in the overall mass measured by the balance.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How does ice (solid state of water) differ from liquid water in terms of shape?

options.label: A
options.text: Ice takes the shape of its container; liquid water has a fixed shape

options.label: B
options.text: Ice has a fixed shape; liquid water takes the shape of its container

options.label: C
options.text: Both ice and liquid water have a fixed shape

options.label: D
options.text: Neither ice nor liquid water has a fixed shape

items.answer: (B) Ice has a fixed shape; liquid water takes the shape of its container. Solids like ice maintain their own definite shape regardless of the container. Liquids like water do not have a fixed shape and will conform to the shape of the container they are in.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How does water vapour (gaseous state) differ from liquid water in terms of spreading and shape?

options.label: A
options.text: Water vapour has a fixed shape; liquid water spreads to fill available space

options.label: B
options.text: Water vapour spreads to fill entire available space and has no fixed shape; liquid water takes container shape but has fixed volume

options.label: C
options.text: Both spread to fill entire available space and have no fixed shape

options.label: D
options.text: Liquid water has a fixed shape; water vapour takes the shape of its container

items.answer: (B) Water vapour spreads to fill entire available space and has no fixed shape; liquid water takes container shape but has fixed volume. Gases like water vapour expand to occupy the entire volume of their container and do not have a definite shape. Liquids take the container’s shape but maintain a constant volume.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the process of conversion of a solid into its liquid state called?

options.label: A
options.text: Freezing

options.label: B
options.text: Evaporation

options.label: C
options.text: Condensation

options.label: D
options.text: Melting

items.answer: (D) Melting Melting is the phase transition process where a substance changes from its solid state to its liquid state, typically upon absorbing heat energy.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Besides water turning into ice, what is another example of a substance changing from liquid to solid (freezing)?

options.label: A
options.text: Liquid wax changing to solid wax upon cooling

options.label: B
options.text: Salt dissolving in water

options.label: C
options.text: Sugar caramelizing upon heating

options.label: D
options.text: Iron rusting in the presence of moisture

items.answer: (A) Liquid wax changing to solid wax upon cooling. Candle wax is an example of a substance that undergoes freezing or solidification—when molten wax cools down, it turns back into a solid form..

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Which condition generally makes water evaporate faster?

options.label: A
options.text: Keeping the water in a narrow-mouthed bottle

options.label: B
options.text: Spreading the water out on a plate (larger exposed surface area)

options.label: C
options.text: Keeping the water in a cool, shaded place

options.label: D
options.text: High humidity in the surrounding air

items.answer: (B) Spreading the water out on a plate (larger exposed surface area). A larger surface area exposed to the air allows more water molecules to escape into the vapour phase simultaneously, thus increasing the rate of evaporation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: On a hot sunny day, clothes dry faster than on a cloudy day. This is primarily because:

options.label: A
options.text: Sunlight makes the clothes heavier

options.label: B
options.text: Higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation

options.label: C
options.text: Sunlight chemically changes the water into gas

options.label: D
options.text: Clouds prevent air movement

items.answer: (B) Higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation. Increased temperature provides more energy to the water molecules in the wet clothes, causing them to transition into water vapour more rapidly, hence speeding up the drying process.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is humidity?

options.label: A
options.text: The speed of the wind

options.label: B
options.text: The temperature of the air

options.label: C
options.text: The amount of water vapour present in the air

options.label: D
options.text: The pressure exerted by the air

items.answer: (C) The amount of water vapour present in the air. Humidity is a measure of the quantity of water vapour contained in the atmosphere or a given volume of air. Higher humidity means more moisture in the air.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Why does water in an earthen pot (matka) often feel colder than water in a stainless steel pot?

options.label: A
options.text: The clay of the earthen pot actively cools the water chemically

options.label: B
options.text: Water seeps through the pores of the earthen pot and evaporates, causing a cooling effect

options.label: C
options.text: Stainless steel heats up the water it contains

options.label: D
options.text: Earthen pots are always kept in colder locations

items.answer: (B) Water seeps through the pores of the earthen pot and evaporates, causing a cooling effect. Earthen pots are porous. Water seeps to the outer surface and evaporates. This evaporation process requires heat, which is drawn from the pot and the water inside, leading to cooling.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How do dust particles in the atmosphere contribute to the formation of clouds?

options.label: A
options.text: Dust particles directly convert into water droplets

options.label: B
options.text: Dust particles provide surfaces for water vapour to condense upon

options.label: C
options.text: Dust particles absorb sunlight, heating the air and forming clouds

options.label: D
options.text: Dust particles repel water vapour, forcing it to accumulate

items.answer: (B) Dust particles provide surfaces for water vapour to condense upon. Water vapour in the air needs a surface to condense into liquid droplets. Tiny dust particles (and other aerosols) act as condensation nuclei, around which water vapour can gather and form cloud droplets.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the water cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: The process of purifying water for drinking

options.label: B
options.text: The seasonal flooding of rivers

options.label: C
options.text: The circulation of water between the Earth’s surface and the atmosphere

options.label: D
options.text: The storage of water in underground reservoirs

items.answer: (C) The circulation of water between the Earth’s surface and the atmosphere. The water cycle describes the continuous movement of water on, above, and below the surface of the Earth, involving processes like evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and runoff.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Which of these is NOT a commonly observed state of water in daily life?

options.label: A
options.text: Solid (ice)

options.label: B
options.text: Liquid (water)

options.label: C
options.text: Gas (water vapour/steam)

options.label: D
options.text: Plasma

items.answer: (D) Plasma Water commonly exists in three states in daily life: solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (water vapour or steam). While plasma is another state of matter, it is not typically observed with water in everyday situations.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is a key difference between evaporation and condensation?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporation is liquid to gas; condensation is gas to liquid

options.label: B
options.text: Evaporation is gas to liquid; condensation is liquid to gas

options.label: C
options.text: Evaporation requires cooling; condensation requires heating

options.label: D
options.text: Both are processes of solid changing to liquid

items.answer: (A) Evaporation is liquid to gas; condensation is gas to liquid. Evaporation is the phase change from liquid to gas (e.g., water to water vapour). Condensation is the opposite phase change, from gas to liquid (e.g., water vapour to water droplets).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Which of these factors generally SLOWS DOWN the rate of evaporation?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased temperature

options.label: B
options.text: Increased wind speed

options.label: C
options.text: Increased surface area of water

options.label: D
options.text: Increased humidity

items.answer: (D) Increased humidity High humidity means the air is already holding a lot of water vapour. This makes it harder for more water to evaporate into the air, thus slowing down the evaporation rate.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: If you want to dry your wet clothes quickly on a day that is not sunny, what could you do to speed up the process, based on the principles of evaporation?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the clothes bundled up tightly

options.label: B
options.text: Place them in a still, closed room

options.label: C
options.text: Use a fan to increase air movement over the clothes

options.label: D
options.text: Sprinkle more water on them

items.answer: (C) Use a fan to increase air movement over the clothes. Increasing air movement (wind) helps to carry away the water vapour forming near the surface of the wet clothes, allowing more water to evaporate more quickly.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Assertion (A) : Ice floats on water. Reason (R) : Ice is the solid state of water and all solids are denser than their liquids.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (C) A is true, but R is false. Ice indeed floats on water. However, the reason is that ice (solid water) is less dense than liquid water, which is an unusual property. Most substances are denser in their solid state than in their liquid state.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Puddles drying up on a sunny day. Which of these involve a change from liquid to gas?

options.label: A
options.text: 1 only

options.label: B
options.text: 3 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: D
options.text: 2 and 3 only

items.answer: (B) 3 only

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Aavi and Thirav are making lemonade on a hot day. They add ice cubes to a glass of lemonade. After a few minutes, they notice the outside of the glass is wet. This wetness is most likely due to:

options.label: A
options.text: Lemonade seeping through tiny cracks in the glass

options.label: B
options.text: The ice melting so fast that it splashes out

options.label: C
options.text: Condensation of water vapour from the humid air onto the cold glass surface

options.label: D
options.text: The glass sweating because it is working hard to keep the lemonade cold

items.answer: (C) Condensation of water vapour from the humid air onto the cold glass surface. The cold surface of the glass, due to the ice and cold lemonade, cools the surrounding humid air. This causes the water vapour in the air to change into liquid water droplets on the glass, a process known as condensation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the term for the state of water when it is invisible and present in the air around us, even at room temperature?

options.label: A
options.text: Ice crystals

options.label: B
options.text: Liquid dew

options.label: C
options.text: Water vapour

options.label: D
options.text: Pressurized steam

items.answer: (C) Water vapour Water vapour is the gaseous state of water. It is present in the air around us, even when not visible, and is a key component of humidity.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: When water is boiled in a kettle and steam comes out, if you hold a cool plate above the steam, water droplets form on the plate. This demonstrates:

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporation from the plate

options.label: B
options.text: Condensation of steam

options.label: C
options.text: Freezing of steam

options.label: D
options.text: Melting of the plate

items.answer: (B) Condensation of steam. The hot steam (water vapour) comes into contact with the cooler surface of the plate, loses heat, and changes its state from gas back to liquid water droplets, which is condensation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: The process by which liquid water changes into solid ice is called:

options.label: A
options.text: Melting

options.label: B
options.text: Evaporation

options.label: C
options.text: Condensation

options.label: D
options.text: Freezing

items.answer: (D) Freezing Freezing, or solidification, is the phase transition where a liquid turns into a solid when its temperature is lowered below its freezing point.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Which of these factors, when increased, typically leads to a slower rate of evaporation?

options.label: A
options.text: Temperature of the water

options.label: B
options.text: Surface area of the water

options.label: C
options.text: Speed of wind blowing over the water

options.label: D
options.text: Humidity of the surrounding air

items.answer: (D) Humidity of the surrounding air Higher humidity means the air is already saturated or nearly saturated with water vapour. This makes it more difficult for additional water to evaporate into the air, thereby slowing down the evaporation process.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How do the properties of shape and ability to flow compare between solid ice and liquid water?

options.label: A
options.text: Ice has a fixed shape and flows; water takes container’s shape and does not flow

options.label: B
options.text: Ice has a fixed shape and does not flow; water takes container’s shape and flows

options.label: C
options.text: Both have fixed shapes and flow easily

options.label: D
options.text: Neither has a fixed shape, but only water flows

items.answer: (B) Ice has a fixed shape and does not flow; water takes container’s shape and flows. Solid ice maintains its own definite shape and does not flow. Liquid water, characteristic of fluids, takes the shape of its container and can flow readily.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: All of the following are examples of evaporation in daily life EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Drying of wet clothes

options.label: B
options.text: Disappearance of water from mopped floors

options.label: C
options.text: Formation of dew drops on grass in the morning

options.label: D
options.text: Sweat drying from our body

items.answer: (C) Formation of dew drops on grass in the morning. Drying clothes, mopped floors, and sweat involve liquid water turning into vapour (evaporation). Dew formation is an example of condensation, where water vapour from the air turns into liquid droplets on cool surfaces.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: 9, what needs to be done regularly to the sand between the pots?

options.label: A
options.text: The sand needs to be replaced with fresh soil daily

options.label: B
options.text: The sand needs to be kept moist by adding water

options.label: C
options.text: The sand should be heated to keep the inner pot warm

options.label: D
options.text: The sand should be covered with a plastic sheet

items.answer: (B) The sand needs to be kept moist by adding water. The cooling effect of the pot-in-pot cooler relies on the evaporation of water from the moist sand. Therefore, water must be added regularly to the sand to maintain moisture for continuous evaporation and cooling.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Assertion (A) : Water vapour is lighter than air, causing it to rise in the atmosphere. Reason (R) : Clouds are formed when this rising water vapour cools and condenses at certain heights.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Water vapour being lighter than the surrounding air causes it to ascend. As it rises to higher altitudes where temperatures are lower, it cools down and undergoes condensation, forming tiny water droplets or ice crystals that constitute clouds.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Still air (no wind)

options.label: A
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 and 3 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 3 only

items.answer: (A) 1 and 2 only Low humidity allows more water to enter the air. High temperature provides more energy for water molecules to escape. Wind (not still air) helps by removing moist air from above the water surface.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: On a cold winter morning, you see your breath as a cloud when you exhale. This visible cloud is formed due to:

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporation of water from your mouth

options.label: B
options.text: Condensation of water vapour from your warm breath in the cold air

options.label: C
options.text: Freezing of air particles

options.label: D
options.text: Smoke particles present in your breath

items.answer: (B) Condensation of water vapour from your warm breath in the cold air. Your warm, moist breath contains water vapour. When this exhaled air mixes with the cold winter air, the water vapour cools rapidly and condenses into tiny visible water droplets or ice crystals, forming the cloud you see.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: The Thirukkural quote at the beginning implies that :

options.label: A
options.text: Oceans will dry up if it gets too hot

options.label: B
options.text: Rain is essential even for the mighty ocean to maintain its level

options.label: C
options.text: Ocean water is the primary source of all rainfall

options.label: D
options.text: It is impossible for the ocean to ever be drained

items.answer: (B) Rain is essential even for the mighty ocean to maintain its level. The quote If it does not rain well, even the mighty ocean will be drained suggests the importance of rainfall in replenishing water bodies, including the vast ocean, implying a connection within the water cycle.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Why does rubbing hand sanitizer on your hands make them feel cool?

options.label: A
options.text: The sanitizer chemically reacts with skin to produce cold

options.label: B
options.text: The sanitizer is stored at a very low temperature

options.label: C
options.text: The alcohol in the sanitizer evaporates quickly, taking heat from your hands

options.label: D
options.text: The sanitizer absorbs water from the skin, causing a cooling sensation

items.answer: (C) The alcohol in the sanitizer evaporates quickly, taking heat from your hands. Hand sanitizer often contain alcohol, which evaporates rapidly at room temperature. This evaporation process requires heat energy, which it draws from the surface of your hands, resulting in a cooling sensation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: The conversion of water from its liquid state to its gaseous state below its boiling point is specifically termed:

options.label: A
options.text: Boiling

options.label: B
options.text: Evaporation

options.label: C
options.text: Sublimation

options.label: D
options.text: Condensation

items.answer: (B) Evaporation Evaporation is the process where a liquid turns into a gas at any temperature below its boiling point, occurring at the surface of the liquid. Boiling is a specific type of rapid vaporization that occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling point.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: In the diagram illustrating the water cycle (Figure), what process is shown occurring from oceans, lakes, and rivers, leading to the formation of water vapour in the atmosphere?

options.label: A
options.text: Condensation

options.label: B
options.text: Precipitation

options.label: C
options.text: Evaporation

options.label: D
options.text: Infiltration

items.answer: (C) Evaporation The diagram of the water cycle would depict water from surface bodies like oceans, lakes, and rivers turning into water vapour and rising into the atmosphere. This process is evaporation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How do the three states of water-ice, liquid water, and water vapour-differ in terms of their ability to flow?

options.label: A
options.text: Only ice can flow

options.label: B
options.text: Only liquid water can flow

options.label: C
options.text: Both liquid water and water vapour can flow; ice cannot

options.label: D
options.text: All three states can flow equally well

items.answer: (C) Both liquid water and water vapour can flow; ice cannot. Liquids (like water) and gases (like water vapour) are fluids, meaning they can flow and take the shape of their container. Solids (like ice) have a fixed shape and do not flow in the same manner.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What are the different forms of the same substance, like ice and water, called?
items.answer: These different forms are also called states.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the gaseous state of water called?
items.answer: The gaseous state of water is called water vapour.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the process of conversion of water into its vapour state called?
items.answer: The process is called evaporation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Is water vapour visible or invisible?
items.answer: Water vapour itself is actually invisible.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Give one example of evaporation from daily life.
items.answer: Drying of wet clothes (or mopped floor, sweat).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What happens to hand sanitizer when you rub it on your hands?
items.answer: Hand sanitizer evaporates from your hands.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What are the tiny drops of water appearing on the outer surface of a cold glass tumbler called?
items.answer: They are called water droplets.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the process of conversion of water vapour into its liquid state called?
items.answer: The process is called condensation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the amount of water vapour in the air also known as?
items.answer: The amount of water vapour in the air is also known as humidity.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Name the solid state of water.
items.answer: The solid state of water is ice.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Does ice flow like water?
items.answer: No, ice does not flow like water.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Does water (liquid state) have a fixed shape?
items.answer: No, water (liquid state) does not have a fixed shape; it takes the shape of the container.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Do gases like water vapour possess a fixed shape?
items.answer: No, gases do not possess a fixed shape and spread out in the entire available space.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Name a substance other than water that can exist in solid, liquid and gaseous states.
items.answer: Wax (or oil, ghee).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What must be supplied to ice to change it into water?
items.answer: Heat must be supplied to ice to change it into water.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the process of conversion of a solid into its liquid state called?
items.answer: The process is called melting.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the process of conversion of a liquid into its solid state called?
items.answer: The process is called freezing.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Name one condition that affects how fast water evaporates.
items.answer: Exposed surface area (or sunlight, wind, humidity).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What effect does evaporation have on the surrounding temperature?
items.answer: Evaporation causes a cooling effect.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is the circulation of water between the Earth’s surface and atmosphere known as?
items.answer: The circulation of water is known as the water cycle.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Are ice and water different substances or different states of the same substance? Explain briefly.
items.answer: Ice and water are different states of the same substance. Ice is the solid state, and water is the liquid state.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Why does water sprinkled on a hot pan disappear quickly? Name the process involved.
items.answer: Water sprinkled on a hot pan disappears quickly because it gets converted into steam (water vapour). The process involved is evaporation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What makes steam visible if water vapour itself is invisible?
items.answer: Steam is visible due to the presence of tiny droplets of water that form when some of the water vapour condenses.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How do dew drops form on plants, especially in the morning?
items.answer: Dew drops form when water vapour present in the air comes in contact with the cool surfaces of plant leaves and condenses into liquid water.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Describe one property of water in its solid state (ice) regarding its shape.
items.answer: Ice (solid state) retains its shape irrespective of the container in which it is placed; it has a fixed shape.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Describe one property of water in its liquid state regarding its shape and volume.
items.answer: Water (liquid state) takes the shape of the container it is in, so it has no fixed shape, but its volume remains constant.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Describe one property of water in its gaseous state (water vapour) regarding its shape and spreading.
items.answer: Water vapour (gaseous state) has no fixed shape and exhibits the property of spreading out to fill the entire available space.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How can the state of water be changed from solid (ice) to liquid, and then from liquid to gas (water vapour)?
items.answer: By supplying heat, ice (solid) melts into water (liquid). On further heating, water (liquid) evaporates or boils into water vapour (gas).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How can the state of water be changed from liquid to solid (ice)? Name this process.
items.answer: Water can be changed to ice by placing it in a cold environment, like a freezer. This process is called freezing.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Explain how increasing the exposed surface area affects the rate of evaporation of water.
items.answer: If water is spread out on a larger surface area, more water molecules are exposed to the air, leading to faster evaporation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How does sunlight affect the rate of evaporation compared to shade?
items.answer: Water evaporates faster when exposed to sunlight compared to when it is kept in the shade because sunlight provides more heat energy.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How does wind affect the rate of drying of clothes? Explain briefly.
items.answer: Clothes dry faster on a windy day because the wind carries away the water vapour from near the clothes, allowing more water to evaporate.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Why do clothes dry slowly on a rainy day?
items.answer: On a rainy day, the air is already high in humidity (water vapour). This slows down the rate of evaporation from clothes.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Explain the cooling effect observed when water evaporates from an earthen pot (matka).
items.answer: Water seeps through the tiny pores of the earthen pot and evaporates from its outer surface. This evaporation draws heat from the pot and the water inside, causing a cooling effect.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Give an example of how the cooling effect of evaporation is used in daily life, apart from the matka.
items.answer: Sprinkling water on the roof or floor during summer cools the area as the water evaporates, taking heat away.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How are clouds formed in the atmosphere?
items.answer: Water vapour in the air rises, cools at higher altitudes, and condenses around tiny dust particles to form small water droplets, which collectively appear as clouds.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What happens to the tiny water droplets in clouds that leads to rain?
items.answer: Many tiny water droplets in clouds join together to form bigger, heavier drops of water. When these drops become too heavy, they fall as rain.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Besides rain, what are the other forms in which condensed water might fall from clouds?
items.answer: Under special conditions, condensed water might also fall as hail or snow from the clouds.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Why is only a small portion of Earth’s water fit for use by plants, animals, and humans?
items.answer: Most of the Earth’s water is in oceans and is saline (salty), which cannot be used directly for drinking or agriculture by most life forms.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What is an Atmospheric Water Generator (AWG) and how does it produce drinkable water?
items.answer: An AWG is a machine that collects water from humid air by condensing the water vapour through cooling, similar to how water droplets form on a cold glass.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Describe the processes of evaporation and condensation. Give one example from daily life where you observe each process.
items.answer: Evaporation is the conversion of a liquid (like water) into its gaseous state (water vapour), often aided by heat. Example: Wet clothes drying in the sun. Condensation is the conversion of a gas (water vapour) into its liquid state, usually upon cooling. Example: Water droplets forming on the outside of a cold drink glass.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Compare the properties of water in its three states – solid (ice), liquid (water), and gas (water vapour) – in terms of shape, ability to flow and ability to spread.
items.answer: Ice (solid) has a fixed shape, does not flow, and does not spread. Water (liquid) takes the shape of its container (no fixed shape), flows easily, and can spread while maintaining a constant volume. Water vapour (gas) has no fixed shape and spreads out to fill the entire available space.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Explain three conditions that can make water evaporate faster. How does each condition contribute to the increased rate of evaporation?
items.answer: 1. Increased surface area : More water molecules are exposed to air, increasing escape.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Describe how an earthen pot (matka) keeps water cool. What scientific principle is involved in this cooling effect?
items.answer: An earthen pot has tiny pores through which a small amount of water seeps to the outer surface. This water evaporates, taking heat energy from the pot and the water inside. This continuous evaporation leads to a cooling effect, keeping the stored water cooler than the surroundings. The principle is ‘evaporation causes cooling’.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Explain the formation of clouds and how they lead to rain, completing a part of the water cycle.
items.answer: Water from oceans, lakes, and rivers evaporates into the atmosphere as water vapour. This vapour rises, and at higher, cooler altitudes, it condenses around dust particles to form tiny water droplets. These droplets gather to form clouds. When the droplets become large and heavy enough, they fall to Earth as rain.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: What are the different states of water? Describe how you can change water from its solid state to liquid and then to gaseous state, and vice-versa, mentioning the names of the processes.
items.answer: Water exists in solid (ice), liquid (water), and gaseous (water vapour) states. Heating ice causes it to melt into water (melting). Further heating water causes it to evaporate or boil into water vapour (evaporation/boiling). Cooling water vapour causes it to condense into liquid water (condensation). Further cooling water causes it to freeze into ice (freezing).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Water vapour is present in the air around us, even though it is invisible. Describe an activity or observation that provides evidence for this statement.
items.answer: Take a glass tumbler and fill it with ice-cold water. After a few minutes, tiny water droplets will appear on the outer surface of the glass. These droplets are formed because the invisible water vapour present in the surrounding air comes into contact with the cold surface of the glass and condenses into liquid water.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Why is it important to use water wisely and avoid wasting it? Mention two ways water gets polluted and why polluted water is a concern.
items.answer: It is important to use water wisely because only a small fraction of Earth’s water is freshwater fit for use, and demand is increasing. Water gets polluted by dumping household/industrial waste and trash into water bodies. Polluted water is unfit for consumption and harms aquatic life and ecosystems.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Thirav observed water puddles disappearing from the playground. He thought it was absorbed by the soil. Aavi later saw water drying from utensils. What is the common process causing water to disappear in both cases, and what other factor might contribute to water disappearing from puddles?
items.answer: The common process is evaporation, where water turns into water vapour. For puddles on the playground, besides evaporation into the air, some water can also seep into the ground (absorption by soil). So, both processes can contribute to the disappearance of water from puddles.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: How does humidity affect the rate of evaporation? Explain why clothes take longer to dry on a day with high humidity.
items.answer: Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. When humidity is high, the air is already saturated or nearly saturated with water vapour. This reduces the rate at which more water can evaporate from surfaces like wet clothes, hence they dry slower.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Aavi’s mother hangs freshly washed clothes outside on a sunny and windy day. She notices the clothes dry much faster than on a cloudy, still day. She also spreads the clothes out on the line rather than keeping them bunched up. (i) Name two conditions present on the sunny and windy day that help the clothes dry faster. (ii) Why does spreading the clothes out help them dry faster? (iii) What is the scientific term for the process by which water from the wet clothes turns into vapour?
items.answer: (i) The two conditions are sunlight (providing heat) and wind (increasing air movement), both of which increase the rate of evaporation. (ii) Spreading the clothes out increases the exposed surface area of the wet fabric, allowing more water to evaporate simultaneously. (iii) The process is called evaporation.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: Thirav takes out a bottle of cold water from the refrigerator and places it on a table. After some time, he observes small droplets of water on the outer surface of the bottle. The water level inside the bottle has not changed. (i) Where do these water droplets on the outer surface of the bottle come from? (ii) Name the process responsible for the formation of these droplets. (iii) Why did the water level inside the bottle not change, even though droplets appeared outside?
items.answer: (i) The water droplets come from the water vapour present in the surrounding air. (ii) The process responsible is condensation. (iii) The water level inside didn’t change because the droplets formed from condensation of external air moisture, not from water seeping out of the sealed bottle.

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: During winter, Aavi notices that the coconut oil kept in a bottle has turned solid. When her mother warms the bottle slightly, the oil turns back into a liquid. (i) What is the process called when liquid coconut oil turns solid in winter? (ii) What is the process called when the solid coconut oil turns back into a liquid upon warming? (iii) Does coconut oil behave similarly to water in terms of changing states with temperature?
items.answer: (i) The process is called freezing (or solidification). (ii) The process is called melting. (iii) Yes, like water, coconut oil changes its state from liquid to solid on cooling (freezing) and from solid to liquid on heating (melting).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: On a hot day, a gardener sprinkles water on the plants and also on the cemented path around the garden. He says this helps to cool the area. (i) How does sprinkling water help to cool the cemented path? (ii) Will the cooling effect be more noticeable on a dry day or a humid day? Why? (iii) What state change is water undergoing when it is sprinkled and then disappears from the path?
items.answer: (i) The sprinkled water evaporates from the hot cemented path. Evaporation is a cooling process as it takes heat from the surface. (ii) The cooling effect will be more noticeable on a dry day because evaporation occurs faster when the air is dry (low humidity). (iii) Water is changing from a liquid state to a gaseous state (water vapour).

items.chapter: A Journey through States of Water
items.stem: A pot of water is put on a stove to boil. As it heats up, steam starts rising. If a cool metal lid is held over the steam for a few moments, tiny water droplets form on the underside of the lid. (i) What process causes steam to rise from the boiling water? (ii) What process causes water droplets to form on the cool metal lid? (iii) Are the steam rising from the pot and the water droplets on the lid different states of water? Identify them.
items.answer: (i) The process causing steam to rise is evaporation (specifically boiling, which is rapid evaporation throughout the liquid). (ii) The process causing water droplets to form on the cool lid is condensation. (iii) Yes, they are different states. The steam contains water in its gaseous state (water vapour), and the droplets on the lid are water in its liquid state.
